title: Scenario cards
subject: Computing
unit: Spring 1: Binary, safety and Boolean logic
source: Seeded from computing/y8 lesson 3 (Scenario cards (pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 3: Staying safe online: risks, cyber abuse and keeping evidence. To understand how to protect our accounts and respond to cyber abuse safely and lawfully

questions.q: A message: 'Your Microsoft account is locked. Log in here within 1 hour.' Name three warning signs.
questions.a: Urgency, a link to log in, an unexpected message (check the sender address too).
questions.model: Teacher underlines: '1 hour' (urgency), 'log in here' (link asking for credentials), not expected (check the real sender address).

questions.a: Logging in with two proofs, such as a password and a code from a phone.

questions.q: Order: report, do not reply, screenshot, tell, block.
questions.a: Do not reply, screenshot, block, report, tell.

questions.q: Core: Read the three scenarios. For each, write the risk, what to do and who to tell, in the portal response box.
questions.a: Each answer names the risk, uses the evidence steps and names a trusted adult.
questions.model: Teacher completes scenario 1: risk (phishing), action (do not click, report), tell (parent and teacher).

questions.q: Extend: Write a paragraph: how does UK law protect people from online abuse? Start: 'In the UK, sending threatening messages...'
questions.a: In the UK, sending threatening or grossly offensive messages can be an offence (Malicious Communications Act 1988), and repeated harassment is a crime (Protection from Harassment Act 1997).

questions.q: Stretch: Explain how Islamic teaching on speech and the evidence steps work together.
questions.a: Islam forbids harming others with words; the steps stop the harm, protect the victim and let adults act justly.

questions.q: Two-factor authentication uses... A) two passwords B) a password and a second proof such as a code C) two usernames
questions.a: B) a password and a second proof such as a code
options: A password and a second proof

questions.q: Big question: if a hurtful message is deleted, has it really gone? Why does it matter for evidence?
questions.a: Not necessarily: others may have saved it; screenshot quickly so adults can act.
